title: 8. Stage 4 Technical Breakdown, Institutional Flow & Stop-Loss Ratchet

epigraph.quote: Never argue with a Stage 4 breakdown, and never lower a held stop-loss to rationalize a losing tape. When price loses both the 50-day and 30-week averages, discipline means protecting capital first.
epigraph.author: Stan Weinstein Tape Discipline

web_blocks.title: Upward-Only Stop-Loss Ratchet & Stage 4 Discipline
paragraphs: TradingView's raw Stage 4 model drops support to ₹1,393.78–₹1,436.22 (200D SMA / S1 ₹1,415.00) with a raw stop at ₹1,385.20. Lowering our held ₹1,539.80 stop to ₹1,385.20 would break our upward-only stop-loss ratchet. Our hard stop stays strictly locked at ₹1,539.80 (-3.80% below ₹1,600.70). We exit via an immediate 90-share trim and a bounce or stop exit on the last 90 shares.

book_paragraphs: If Chapter 7 established that Astra Microwave's 70.61x multiple leaves zero margin of safety against Bharat Electronics and HAL, Chapter 8 delivers the verdict of the tape itself—and the tape has decisively deteriorated since our November 13 review. Back on November 13, Astra Microwave traded at ₹1,703.50 in Stage 3 topping, above its 50-day and 30-week averages, while flashing six distribution days as an early warning. Over the last two weeks, that warning converted into an outright breakdown.

Let us walk through both verified checkpoints with precision. On the verified November 23, 2026 NSE market-facts ledger, Astra Microwave closed at ₹1,623.30, down 1.18 percent on a session when the Nifty 50 dropped 1.75 percent to 25,349.65 under an Uptrend (narrow breadth) regime with 55.2 percent of Nifty 500 stocks above their 50-day average. At that November 23 close, the ledger still classified Astra Microwave as Stage 3 (Topping / Pullback), but the internal damage was already severe: the 50-day simple moving average was falling/flat at ₹1,625.27 (down from ₹1,662.76 twenty-one trading days earlier), the stock carried six distribution days in twenty-five sessions, and its 28-day relative strength had plunged to minus 17.29 percent (minus 8.23 percent over 63 days).

Two sessions later, on the November 25, 2026 live TradingView snapshot, the structural floor gave way. Astra Microwave fell another 1.39 percent to ₹1,600.70—down 4.26 percent on the week, down 6.23 percent over three months, and down 18.33 percent from its ₹1,960.00 52-week peak. More importantly, ₹1,600.70 sits below EVERY short- and medium-term institutional trend line: 1.27 percent below the 50-day SMA (₹1,621.36), 1.31 percent below the 10-week EMA (₹1,621.93), and 0.40 percent below the critical 30-week SMA (₹1,607.16). Under Stan Weinstein's stage framework, closing beneath both a rolling 50-day average and the 30-week average triggers a formal downgrade to Stage 4—AVOID_STAGE4_OR_BROKEN—with a hard technical ceiling of CAP_REJECTED for all fresh capital.

The multi-timeframe momentum indicators confirm there is no reversal underway yet. On the November 25 live snapshot, 14-period RSI reads 52.55 on the weekly chart, 46.04 on the daily chart, and 40.81 on the 4-hour chart. Price sits beneath both the 4-hour 20-EMA (₹1,642.39) and the 4-hour 50-SMA (₹1,605.08), flagging no intraday 4-hour turn. Meanwhile, daily volume shrank to 148,112 shares—just 0.41 times the 30-day average of 357,539 shares—showing that institutional dip-buyers have stepped aside rather than defending the 30-week average. Contrast that tape with Bharat Electronics (Stage 2 at ₹404.30, +2.82 percent above its 10-week EMA, 1.13x volume) and Hindustan Aeronautics (Stage 2 at ₹4,936.00, +2.00 percent above its 10-week EMA, 1.26x volume). Money is rotating inside Indian defense away from cash-hungry, high-multiple subcontractors and back into debt-free, high-ROCE primes.

Shareholding and market-structure dynamics explain why this breakdown demands immediate action on our held shares. Between June and September 2026, domestic mutual funds and DIIs raised their stake from 15.42 percent to 16.52 percent while FIIs edged down from 10.74 percent to 10.48 percent. However, promoters own only 6.54 percent of the equity, and Q2 FY27 exchange filings revealed that Whole-Time Director of Strategy Atim Kabra trimmed his personal holding by 0.41 percentage points to 3.12 percent (29.64 lakh shares). Add the fact that Astra Microwave is not in the NSE F&O segment—meaning zero listed protective puts, zero covered-call income, and zero options hedging—and every rupee of exposure sits unprotected in cash equity.

Now let us address the single most important risk-management rule for our 180 Zerodha shares: the upward-only stop-loss ratchet. Because Astra Microwave has broken below its 30-week average, TradingView's automated Stage 4 model drops its next structural support shelf down to the 200-day SMA and Pivot S1 near ₹1,393.78–₹1,436.22 (₹1,415.00 S1), with a raw technical invalidation stop at ₹1,385.20. A undisciplined investor looks at ₹1,385.20 and says, 'Let me move my stop down to the 200-day average to give it more room.' We strictly forbid that. Moving a held stop-loss downward from ₹1,539.80 to ₹1,385.20 turns a controlled tactical trade into a 15-to-18 percent portfolio wound right as fundamentals weaken.

Instead, our binding upward-only stop-loss ratchet locks the hard stop strictly at ₹1,539.80—preserving the exact prior floor, just 3.80 percent (roughly 1.02 times the ₹59.60 daily ATR) below the live ₹1,600.70 close. On the upside, the broken 50-day SMA (₹1,621.36), 10-week EMA (₹1,621.93), 4-hour 20-EMA (₹1,642.39), and Pivot R1 (₹1,670.20) now form a thick ceiling of overhead supply. That technical map hands us an exact execution blueprint for Chapter 9: trim half the position immediately into current liquidity, and use any relief bounce into ₹1,621–₹1,670—or a daily close below ₹1,539.80—to exit the rest cleanly.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The biggest mistake in momentum investing is lowering your stop-loss after a stock enters Stage 4. Locking our held stop strictly at ₹1,539.80—refusing to drop it to ₹1,385.20—keeps a broken chart from becoming a permanent capital loss.
